label: More on the Geometry of H^n
notes: Open by stressing that hyperbolic space is one object wearing several costumes. Across printed pages 81 to 96 we will move a single geodesic between four models, so the audience learns that a circular arc and a straight chord can describe the very same line under different coordinates.

label: Four Models, One Space
notes: Name the four charts and what each privileges. The hyperboloid carries the algebra, the ball and half-space carry conformal pictures, and the Klein disk makes geodesics into chords. Emphasise that isometries between models are explicit maps, so any theorem proved in one chart transfers verbatim to the others.

label: The Hyperboloid Model
notes: Introduce the Lorentzian form of signature (n,1) and the upper sheet where it equals minus one. Distance comes from the inner product through an inverse hyperbolic cosine. Point out that this model is where the isometry group O(n,1) acts most transparently, by linear maps preserving the quadratic form.

label: The Poincare Ball
notes: Write the conformal metric on the open unit ball and note the factor that blows up near the boundary, which pushes the rim to infinite distance. Stress conformality: hyperbolic angles equal Euclidean angles here, which is exactly why geodesics meet the bounding sphere orthogonally.

label: Geodesics as Orthogonal Arcs
notes: Walk through the picture: diameters and circular arcs perpendicular to the boundary are the geodesics. Have students verify orthogonality by eye on the diagram. Tie this to the inversion that fixes the boundary circle, which is the geometric reason the right angle is forced.

label: Upper Half-Space and Klein
notes: Contrast the half-space, where geodesics are vertical rays and semicircles centred on the boundary plane, with the Klein disk, where geodesics become honest straight chords at the price of losing conformality. The Cayley-type transforms linking these charts are the dictionary entries we keep returning to.

label: The Isometry Group O(n,1)
notes: Identify the full isometry group with the projective Lorentz group, generated by reflections in hyperplanes. Mention the Mobius description in the ball and half-space: isometries are conformal maps preserving the boundary. Reflections generating the group is the recurring structural fact worth memorising.

label: The Boundary at Infinity
notes: Define boundary points as equivalence classes of asymptotic geodesic rays, and identify the resulting sphere at infinity with the bounding sphere of the ball model. Stress that isometries extend continuously to this sphere, acting as conformal homeomorphisms, which seeds the later study of limit sets.

label: Horospheres and Horoballs
notes: Describe a horosphere as a limit of spheres whose centre escapes to a boundary point, appearing as a sphere internally tangent to the bounding sphere. The region it bounds is a horoball. Contrast horospheres with equidistant hypersurfaces and genuine hyperspheres, which are the three companion families.

label: Busemann Functions
notes: Introduce the Busemann function attached to a ray as the renormalised limit of distance functions. Its level sets are horospheres and its sublevel sets are horoballs. Emphasise that the gradient flow points toward the boundary point, giving a clean analytic handle on the geometry near infinity.

label: Exponential Divergence
notes: Make the curvature minus one consequence vivid: two geodesics from a common point separate at an exponential rate set by the hyperbolic sine of the travelled distance. Contrast with the linear spread of Euclidean rays. This single inequality is the engine behind thin triangles and hyperbolicity.

label: Synthesis and Dictionary
notes: Close by replaying the model dictionary as an audit table linking each chart to its geodesic picture and its native advantage. Remind the class that the notebook artifact tracks one geodesic across charts, and invite them to predict which straight line becomes which arc before checking.
